extraction.name: TextVQA
extraction.description: A visual question answering dataset containing 45,336 questions on 28,408 images that require reading and reasoning about text in images. Each question-image pair has 10 human-provided ground truth answers.
extraction.creator: Amanpreet Singh, Vivek Natarajan, Meet Shah, Yu Jiang, Xinlei Chen, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, Marcus Rohrbach
extraction.citeAs: Amanpreet Singh, Vivek Natarajan, Meet Shah, Yu Jiang, Xinlei Chen, Dhruv Batra, Devi Parikh, and Marcus Rohrbach. Towards VQA Models That Can Read. arXiv:1904.08920v2 [cs.CL], 13 May 2019.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Images were selected from Open Images v3. The authors sampled 100 random images per category, or all images when fewer than 100 were available, ran Rosetta OCR, and used normalized average OCR box counts as category sampling weights. A three-stage crowdsourcing pipeline identified images containing text, collected 1–2 questions per image requiring reading and reasoning about that text, and collected 10 answers per question. Training and validation images came from the Open Images training set; test images came from its test set.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Rosetta returned zero OCR tokens for approximately 1,500 images because it was unable to detect text. The authors manually verified that these images actually contained text.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images from the Open Images v3 dataset, together with crowdsourced questions and answers. Image categories likely to contain text included billboards, traffic signs, and whiteboards.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Questions collected from the Open Images v3 training set were randomly divided into training and validation sets. TextVQA contains 34,602 training questions, 5,000 validation questions, and 5,734 test questions, with no image overlap between splits.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images flagged as having no text and noisy annotations were filtered out. Questions were removed when a majority of workers flagged no text in the image, not a question, answering without reading text, or unanswerability. Hand-crafted questions with known answers were used to identify and filter out bad annotators. For the reported experiments, questions and OCR sequences used maximum lengths of 14 words and 50 tokens, respectively, with shorter sequences padded.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators first indicated whether images contained text using a forced-choice yes/no flag. They then wrote a question requiring reading the image text; inference or paraphrasing was permitted. For a second question, annotators saw the first question and were instructed to provide a different question requiring reasoning about text and having a different answer. Ten human answers were collected per question. Answer annotators could flag images without text, invalid questions, questions not requiring reading, or unanswerable questions. Known-answer questions were used for annotator quality control.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A three-stage annotation interface is shown in Figures 8–11, covering text detection, question collection, and answer collection. No platform name is stated.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Questions were excluded when a majority of answer annotators selected a quality-control flag. The paper analyzes majority answers and inter-annotator agreement: all 10 annotators agreed on the most common answer for 22.8% of questions, and at least three agreed for 97.9%. Evaluation used the VQA accuracy metric; reported human accuracy was 85.01% on validation and 86.79% on test.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 10 human ground truth answers per question-image pair; 1–2 questions were collected per image.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Questions were asked by sighted humans.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Rosetta OCR was used to detect text, compute category sampling weights, and produce OCR word tokens.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The answer space includes people's names, cities, and countries. Dataset examples include a vehicle license number and a birthday date. The paper does not describe these as systematically collected personal attributes.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset targets reading and reasoning capabilities important for assistive applications for visually impaired users. The paper notes that questions involving reading text are a dominant category of questions these users ask about images of their surroundings.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Images were deliberately sampled toward categories containing text using OCR-derived category weights. Most questions start with 'what'. The most common majority answer, 'yes', accounts for 4.71% of the dataset, and yes/no majority answers account for 5.55%. Question-only and image-only baselines achieved 8.09% and 6.29% validation accuracy, which the authors interpret as indicating no significant biases with respect to images and questions.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The OCR system can fail on rotated, unstructured, or partially occluded text and returned no tokens for approximately 1,500 images that contained text. The diverse answer space includes rare and unseen words, making fixed answer vocabularies limiting. Some questions require combining multiple OCR tokens; 8.9% can only be answered by combining multiple tokens.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of visual question answering models that read and reason about text in natural everyday images. The dataset is intended to benchmark progress complementary to VQA 2.0 and encourage research on text detection and recognition in unconstrained environments.
